children: A server rack packed with Nvidia's (NVDA) most powerful Blackwell Ultra chips, which CEO Jensen Huang once described as too big to smuggle, has reportedly turned up at a data center in Shanghai, adding to scrutiny over the company's restricted chip exports to China.

Chinese loan filings reviewed by Bloomberg show the rack was installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project, a data center linked to Alice Huang, founder of Singapore-based Megaspeed. However, the publication said it found no evidence that Megaspeed itself sent hardware to the Shanghai site. The company has denied wrongdoing.
The company became Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia and is
over concerns it helped smuggle Nvidia chips into China. The Trump administration added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist this month.
rose as much as 2.5% in pre-market trade on Friday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the AI bellwether trended in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day.
Megaspeed and Nvidia had not responded to Stocktwits’ request for comment at the time of writing.
Jensen Huang Has Previously Dismissed Chip Smuggling Concerns

“Our data center GPUs are massive. These are massive systems. The Grace Blackwell system is nearly two tons, so you’re not going to be putting that into your pocket or your backpack anytime soon,” Huang told reporters in a May 2025 interview. “These systems are fairly easy to keep track of but the important thing is that the countries and the companies that we sell to recognize that diversion is not allowed.
“Trying to cobble together data centers with some smuggled products is a dead end,” Huang said more recently, during Nvidia’s June shareholders meeting.
The equipment reportedly found in Shanghai is a GB300 NVL72 rack, roughly the size of a large refrigerator, standing about two meters tall and weighing more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds).

It contains 72 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra chips, which require U.S. export licenses to ship to China. President Donald Trump and his administration have repeatedly said they do not want the chips going to China for now.
Loan Filings Reveal Restricted Nvidia Hardware At Shanghai Site

The hardware came to light through financing records reviewed by Bloomberg. Shanghai Shuoyao, a service provider to Megaspeed, pledged the GB300 rack as collateral for a CN¥96 million ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank.
A separate company, Shanghai Kezhan, disclosed a server containing Nvidia GB200 chips at the same site while securing a CN¥90 million loan from a leasing firm owned by a Shanghai government agency.

According to the report, filings suggest some Chinese lenders, including state-linked institutions, were aware that restricted Nvidia hardware was in the country and were willing to accept it as collateral for loans.
SMCI, DELL Gets Pulled Into Nvidia Controversy

Bloomberg traced the GB300 rack's serial number to Taiwan's Gigabyte Technology, which assembles Nvidia chips into servers. Gigabyte declined to identify the original buyer, saying it complies with applicable laws.

The report added that the equipment may have changed hands multiple times before reaching China. Restricted hardware can move through intermediaries and buyers in countries where exports are not subject to the same restrictions, making its final destination difficult to trace.

Other Nvidia hardware also surfaced in the filings. A sister company of Shanghai Shuoyao disclosed servers containing older Hopper-generation chips manufactured by Super Micro Computer (SMCI) and Dell Technologies (DELL). The report said it remains unclear whether those shipments had U.S. export approval.
Shanghai Kezhan also reported 32 servers containing Nvidia H200 chips at the site.

gained nearly 4% in pre-market trade, while DELL stock rose as much as 4.5%. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around SMCI trended in ‘bearish’ territory over the past day, while sentiment around DELL trended in ‘extremely bullish’ territory.
Massive China Data Center Adds To Nvidia's Export-Control Scrutiny

The Yangtze River Delta Project is planned to house as many as 800,000 servers, putting it on a scale comparable to some of the world's largest AI data centers used by companies such as OpenAI. Bloomberg reported that meeting the project's performance targets would be extremely difficult using domestic Chinese chips from Huawei alone.

The report adds to Nvidia's export-control scrutiny just days after Huang returned as CEO. The company has faced mounting questions over whether its chips are being diverted to China through a shadow market that U.S. officials believe is worth billions of dollars.
Huang is scheduled for a closed-door House interview on December 1 and a public Senate Banking Committee hearing on December 3.
NVDA stock has fallen around 20% this year, not accounting for its pre-market move.

Other Nvidia hardware was also disclosed at the site, including Hopper-generation servers made by Dell Technologies and Super Micro Computer.
Chinese loan filings revealed the hardware after a Megaspeed service provider pledged the rack as collateral for a CN¥96 million loan.
The findings add to scrutiny over Nvidia's ability to prevent restricted chips from reaching China through intermediaries and the secondary market.

title: Jensen Huang Said Blackwell Racks Wouldn't Fit In A 'Pocket Or Backpack' But One Has Reportedly Turned Up in Shanghai
